topic: Recap: what a block, a hash and a node each do
title: Bitcoin Mining Recap: Blocks, Hashes and Nodes
hook: Three words explain most of Bitcoin mining.

scenes.narration: A block is a batch of transactions. Its header stores the hash of the previous block, which links blocks into a chain.
Miners hash the block header over and over, looking for a result that does not exceed the network's target.
Full nodes independently validate every block using the same rules, so miners cannot simply write their own.

cta: If this helped, the link in my description goes deeper on digital mining.
description_body: A quick recap of three core ideas: blocks link to each other, hashes are the search, and nodes check the result.

topic: What miners change to get a new hash: the nonce
title: What Is a Nonce in Bitcoin Mining?
hook: Miners keep changing one tiny number. Here is why.

scenes.narration: Hash the same block header twice and you get the same answer, so a miner has to change something to try again.
The block header has an easy-to-modify nonce field. Changing it gives a brand new hash to test.
Each new hash is compared with the network target. If it does not exceed it, the block is valid proof of work.

cta: Curious how digital mining fits in? The link is in the description.
description_body: The nonce is the field miners adjust to produce new hashes until one meets the network target.

topic: Myth: miners can approve any transactions they like
title: Myth: Can Bitcoin Miners Approve Anything?
hook: Can a miner just add any transaction they want?

scenes.narration: Some people think whoever mines a block decides what is valid. That is not how Bitcoin works.
Each full node independently validates blocks using the same consensus rules.
Nodes accept a block only if all its transactions are valid and not already spent.

cta: More mining basics are waiting, and the link is in the description.
description_body: Miners propose blocks, but full nodes validate them. A block with invalid or already-spent transactions is not accepted.

title: How Bitcoin Mining Difficulty Adjusts
hook: Bitcoin changes its own difficulty. Here is how.

scenes.narration: Every 2,016 blocks, the network checks how long those blocks took, using the timestamps in each block header.
The target is about two weeks. If blocks came too fast, difficulty rises, by as much as 300 percent.
If blocks came too slowly, difficulty falls, by as much as 75 percent. That keeps block time near ten minutes.

cta: Want the bigger picture? The link is in my description.
description_body: Difficulty is recalculated every 2,016 blocks to keep block time near ten minutes, and it can move up or down.

topic: GoMining: what you hold is not the hardware
title: GoMining Digital Miners: What You Actually Hold
hook: A digital miner is not a machine you can touch.

scenes.narration: According to a Forklog explainer, a GoMining digital miner is an NFT representing a share of hashrate hosted in GoMining's data centres.
Owners are credited daily bitcoin rewards. They do not hold the underlying hardware, and miners are not redeemable for bitcoin.
Rewards and maintenance charges move with the bitcoin price, difficulty and hashrate, so net results vary and can be low or negative.

cta: Do your own research first. The link in my description is a starting point.
description_body: What a GoMining digital miner represents, what owners receive, and why results vary. Based on a third-party explainer; check gomining.com for current details.

topic: Where new bitcoin comes from: the first transaction in a block
title: Where Does New Bitcoin Come From?
hook: Every new bitcoin starts in the same place.

scenes.narration: The first transaction in a block is a special transaction that starts a new coin.
Transaction fees are added to the block's incentive value, so the winning miner collects both.
New issuance is not endless. Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million coins.

cta: More short lessons like this are coming, and the link is in the description.
description_body: New coins enter circulation through a special first transaction in each block, alongside fees, within a 21 million cap.
